notes.b: A family's priorities, resources and ability to take part in household tasks change as its members age.
points: Stages include a newly married couple, a family with young children, a family with school-going children, a family with teenagers and an older couple whose children have left home.
Young children need time, money and space for feeding, care and supervision, so childcare and daily routines become central to management.
Older children can take on tasks and join family decisions, which reduces the workload on parents.
Teenagers increase the family's spending on clothing, books, school costs and leisure, and they need planning for further education.
Older people may have a reduced income and reduced mobility, which affects choices about food, transport and housing.
Newly married couples and childless households often have more flexible time and more income for leisure than families with young children.

notes.b: The way family members work determines how much money the family has and when its members are free to carry out tasks.
points: A dual-income household has more money available but less time for housework and meal preparation.
A single-income household has less money to manage, so budgeting and planning for essentials are more critical.
Full-time, part-time, job-sharing, flexible and seasonal hours each change when family members are available for tasks.
Shift work and night work change meal times and sleep patterns, and routines must be built around them.
Commuting adds travel time and cost, which affects the family budget and the time left for household work.
Working from home, or a parent working abroad, changes how tasks and childcare are shared.
A dual role arises when both partners work outside the home, so extra planning is needed for childcare, meals and housework.
A lone parent carries both the earner role and the parent role, with no second adult to share tasks or decisions.
Dual roles need delegation and shared planning, such as a weekly planning meeting or a shared calendar.
Culture shapes family management through dress codes, the food a family eats, religious practices, and festivals and celebrations.
Culture also shapes expectations about who does which tasks and who is expected to earn income.
Values are a family's beliefs about what matters, such as health, sustainability, education, faith or community.
Values determine decisions, such as buying local food, choosing organic produce or reducing waste.
Values change when circumstances change, for example after the illness of a family member.
Standards are the levels of quality a family sets for its home, meals, appearance and finances, such as how clean the house is kept.
Standards determine how much time, money and effort a task requires.
High standards can cause strain and overload when time and resources are limited; low standards can affect health and comfort.
Sex roles are the behaviour expected of men and women within a household.
Traditional sex roles assigned household work to women and income-earning to men; gender roles are increasingly equal, with shared childcare, cooking and cleaning.
When one partner is expected to carry all household tasks, the workload becomes unfair and management is harder to share.

notes.h: Lifestyle: socio-economic status and family composition
notes.b: Lifestyle is the everyday pattern of work, leisure, eating and travel that a family follows; it is shaped by socio-economic status and family composition.
points: Socio-economic status affects income, which sets the total resources available to the family and the choices it can make.
Families from lower socio-economic backgrounds give priority to essentials such as food, heating and housing.
Families from higher socio-economic backgrounds may place more emphasis on luxuries, leisure and extra services.
Socio-economic group also influences educational opportunity and the type of employment available, which in turn affects income.
Family composition is the number and make-up of the people in the family, including the number of children and whether it is a lone-parent or two-parent household.
A larger family needs more food, clothing and space, so budgets and meal plans must be scaled up.
A family member with a disability or special needs can increase household costs and reduce the time or ability of others to earn.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of stages a family passes through over time, each with different priorities and resource needs.
The way family members work, including the number of earners, hours worked and where the work takes place.
The situation where a family member must combine paid work outside the home with the responsibilities of a parent or home manager.
The shared customs, food, dress, religious practices and celebrations that shape how a family lives and manages its home.
A family's beliefs about what matters most, which guide its decisions.
The levels of quality a family sets for its home, meals, appearance and finances.
The behaviour and responsibilities expected of men and women within a household.
A family's position based on its income, occupation and education, which affects the resources it has.
The number and make-up of the people in a family, including children and members with special needs.
The everyday pattern of work, leisure, eating and travel that a family follows.

factCards.term: Five typical stages of the family life cycle
factCards.definition: Newly married couple; family with young children; family with school-going children; family with teenagers; older couple after the children have left home.

factCards.term: Three effects of young children on family management
factCards.definition: Their needs for time, money and space increase; childcare and routines must be planned; daily timetables and budgets are built around their care.

factCards.term: Three effects of shift work on household management
factCards.definition: Meal times change; sleep patterns change; routines must be built around the shift pattern.

factCards.term: Four ways culture can affect family management
factCards.definition: Dress code; the food eaten; religious practices; festivals and celebrations.

factCards.term: Three ways a family's values can change how it is managed
factCards.definition: Choosing local shopping; choosing organic or sustainable food; changing priorities when circumstances change, such as illness.
Number of people in the family; presence of members with special needs; number of children; whether it is a lone-parent or two-parent household.

factCards.term: Two ways a dual-income household differs from a single-income household
factCards.definition: It has more money for spending, saving and credit repayments; it has less time for household tasks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a family's stage in the life cycle affects the management of its home. Give two examples.
questions.model: Two points at 3 marks each. Young children need time, money and space for care, so childcare and daily routines must be planned around them. Teenagers increase spending on clothing, books and school costs and need planning for further education; older children can take on tasks and join family decisions, reducing the parents' workload. Any two well-explained examples with a clear link to management earn full marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss how employment patterns and culture affect the management of a family's resources. Use examples from family life in your answer.
questions.model: Employment patterns: a dual-income household has more money but less time, so planning, delegation and shared tasks are needed; a single-income household has less money, so budgeting for essentials is critical. Shift work changes meal times and sleep patterns, so routines are built around the shift pattern. Commuting adds time and cost to the budget. Culture: food, dress code, religious practices and festivals shape spending and the timing of tasks; culture also shapes expectations of who does which tasks and who earns income. Link: a family that works shifts and follows a religious festival calendar must plan its meals, budget and time around both, combining the influence of employment and culture on its resource management.
